title: THE FAMILY TREE THEY WOULD HAVE HIDDEN… BUT GOD PUT IT ON THE FIRST PAGE OF JESUS’ STORY
paragraphs: THE FAMILY TREE THEY WOULD HAVE HIDDEN… BUT GOD PUT IT ON THE FIRST PAGE OF JESUS’ STORY

Before Jesus performed a miracle, healed a sinner, or preached a sermon, His genealogy revealed something astonishing: God was not ashamed to bring the Savior into a family history filled with broken people, unlikely outsiders, fallen kings, and stories that polite society would rather forget.
What if I told you that one of the most powerful revelations of God's grace is hidden in the part of the Bible most Christians skip?
Not the crucifixion.
Not the empty tomb.
Not the woman caught in adultery.
A genealogy.
A long list of names that many believers have read once, struggled to pronounce, and quietly passed over to get to the birth of Jesus.
But what if those names were never meant to be skipped?
What if Matthew placed them at the very beginning of his Gospel because, before telling us what Jesus came to do, he wanted us to understand the kind of world Jesus came to save?
And what if some of the people in that family tree had stories painfully similar to yours?
A family with secrets.
A past that refuses to stay buried.
A betrayal that changed everything.
A relationship that left wounds nobody sees.
A decision you wish you could undo.
A reputation you have spent years trying to escape.
You may have looked at your family history and wondered whether anything beautiful could ever come from it.
Matthew opens his Gospel with an answer.
And he does not begin with perfect people.
He begins with Jesus Christ.
"The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." — Matthew 1:1 (KJV)
That opening sentence is more revolutionary than it first appears.
In the original Greek, Matthew begins with the words Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ — Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou.
Literally, "Book of the genealogy" or "record of the origin of Jesus Christ."
The expression biblos geneseōs echoes language found in the Greek Old Testament, particularly Genesis 2:4 and 5:1.
Matthew is doing more than presenting a family record.
He is introducing the Messiah in language that recalls beginnings, generations, and God's unfolding work in history.
The Greek word geneseōs is related to the word from which we get "Genesis."
That connection is worth noticing.
The first book of Scripture tells us how humanity began and how sin entered human experience.
Matthew begins his Gospel by introducing the One through whom God's promises of redemption reach their fulfillment.
Not because Jesus was merely another descendant in a long line of descendants.
But because He was the promised Christ.
The Greek word Christos means "Anointed One," corresponding to the Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (Mashiach) — Messiah.
Matthew identifies Jesus as the Son of David and the Son of Abraham because God's promises were never forgotten.
To Abraham, God promised that through his offspring the nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18).
To David, God promised an enduring royal dynasty (2 Samuel 7:12–16).
And now Matthew declares that Jesus stands at the fulfillment of those covenant promises.
But here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
God's faithfulness did not depend on every generation being faithful.
Read that again.
God's faithfulness did not depend on every generation being faithful.
Because if it did, the genealogy would have ended long before Bethlehem.
Matthew could have presented Jesus' ancestry as a polished royal record.
Instead, he deliberately includes details that make the reader stop.
He names Judah and his brothers.
He names Tamar.
He names Rahab.
He names Ruth.
He identifies Solomon through "her that had been the wife of Urias."
He includes kings whose reigns were marked by obedience and kings whose disobedience brought devastation.
He records the Babylonian exile, one of the darkest national tragedies in Israel's history.
And somehow, through all those generations, the story moves toward Jesus.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because injustice did not matter.
Not because God approved of everything these people did.
But because human failure could not overturn God's redemptive purpose.
And the first shocking story appears earlier than many readers expect.
"And Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar." — Matthew 1:3 (KJV)
Judah. Tamar. Perez. Zerah.
Four names in one short statement.
But behind those names is a family story filled with grief, injustice, deception, and moral failure.

Genesis 38 tells us that Tamar had been married into Judah's family. After the deaths of Judah's two older sons, Judah failed to fulfill his obligation to provide for her future through his surviving son.
Tamar was left vulnerable.
Later, she disguised herself, and Judah, not recognizing her, had sexual relations with her.
When her pregnancy became known, Judah initially condemned her.
Then the evidence exposed his own involvement.
And Judah spoke words that still confront hypocrisy thousands of years later:
"She hath been more righteous than I." — Genesis 38:26 (KJV)
Think about that.
The man ready to condemn another person was forced to confront his own wrongdoing.

The story does not present deception or sexual misconduct as virtues. It exposes Judah's failure, Tamar's vulnerability, and the injustice of a man who was prepared to judge someone while concealing his own guilt.
Yet Matthew does not erase Tamar from the record.
Her name remains.
And through Perez, the family line continues toward David and ultimately toward Christ.
Can you imagine the uncomfortable silence if that story were read aloud at a gathering where everyone was trying to protect the family's reputation?
Some families survive by refusing to talk about what happened.
Scripture does not always give us that luxury.
It brings hidden things into the light.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to have someone condemn you while refusing to acknowledge the harm they caused.
Perhaps you have watched people protect appearances while ignoring justice.
Or perhaps you recognize yourself in Judah — quick to notice someone else's failure, slow to confess your own.
Either way, this story refuses to flatter us.
God's grace does not require us to pretend that sin is righteousness.
It calls us to face the truth.
Because repentance begins where excuses end.
Then Matthew introduces another woman.
"And Salmon begat Booz of Rachab." — Matthew 1:5 (KJV)
Rahab.
For some readers, that name immediately recalls a single word.
Prostitute.
Joshua 2 identifies Rahab as a prostitute living in Jericho.
But that is not where her story ends.
When Israel's spies entered Jericho, Rahab protected them because she had come to recognize the power and authority of the God of Israel.
Listen to her confession:
"For the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath." — Joshua 2:11 (KJV)
Rahab was not born into Israel.
She belonged to a city facing judgment.
Her past was complicated.
Her future looked uncertain.
Yet she responded to what she had heard about the Lord with faith.
Hebrews 11:31 remembers her faith.
James 2:25 points to her actions as evidence of that faith.
And Matthew places her name in the genealogy of Jesus.
Consider the significance.
The woman once identified by her former occupation is remembered in Scripture for trusting the living God.
Her past is not denied.
But neither is it allowed to be the final word about her.
That is not permission to romanticize sin.
It is evidence that God's mercy can reach people whom society has already written off.
Maybe someone still calls you by a name connected to your worst season.
Maybe they remember what you did before you encountered Christ.
Maybe they speak as though your past has the authority to cancel your future.
But the Gospel announces something far greater than the power of a reputation.
"If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
Notice what Paul says.
Not that the past never happened.
Not that consequences magically disappear.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
He says that those who are in Christ belong to a new creation.
A new identity rooted in the Savior, not in the shame that once defined them.
And if that truth is reaching a place in your heart you have kept hidden, do not rush past it.
You are not beyond the reach of the Savior.
Then comes Ruth.
"And Booz begat Obed of Ruth." — Matthew 1:5 (KJV)
Ruth was a Moabite widow.
An outsider by nationality.
A woman who had experienced loss and faced an uncertain future.
Her story is not primarily a scandal. It is a beautiful account of covenant loyalty, faithful love, and God's providential care.
When Naomi urged her to return to her people, Ruth responded:
"Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." — Ruth 1:16 (KJV)
Ruth left what was familiar.
She entered a land where she was a foreigner.
She gathered leftover grain to survive.
She did not know how the story would end.
But through God's providence, Boaz became her husband, Obed was born, and Obed became the grandfather of David.
And generations later, Matthew names Ruth in the ancestry of Jesus.
Why does this matter?
Because the promised blessing to Abraham was never intended to remain a private possession of one ethnic family.
God had promised blessing to the nations.
Ruth's presence anticipates that wider purpose.
She was not included because her ancestry was impressive.
She was included within the unfolding covenant story through which God would bring the Messiah.
Perhaps you have spent much of your life feeling like an outsider.
The one who did not belong.
The one who arrived late.
The one whose background made people uncomfortable.
The one who felt unwelcome even in places where love should have been obvious.
Ruth's story reminds us that God is not limited by the social boundaries people construct.
And in Jesus Christ, people from every nation are invited to turn to God through faith.
Then Matthew arrives at a sentence that should make every reader uncomfortable.
"And David the king begat Solomon of her that had been the wife of Urias." — Matthew 1:6 (KJV)
Matthew does not even name Bathsheba here.
Instead, he reminds us that she had been the wife of Uriah.
Why mention Uriah?
Because the royal history of David's family cannot be told truthfully without acknowledging what happened.
Second Samuel 11 records David's abuse of royal power, his taking of Bathsheba, and his attempt to conceal what followed.
When Bathsheba became pregnant, David tried to manipulate the circumstances.
When those attempts failed, he arranged for Uriah to be placed in a position where he would be killed in battle.
Uriah died.
David took Bathsheba as his wife.
And for a time, the king continued as though he could manage the consequences.
But Scripture says:
"But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." — 2 Samuel 11:27 (KJV)
Do not miss that sentence.
David was Israel's king.
A man remembered for his faith.
A man through whose royal line the Messiah would come.
Yet none of that made his sin acceptable.
God did not excuse David because he was anointed.
God did not ignore the suffering David caused because he was important.
And God did not call evil good simply because it happened within the royal family.
The prophet Nathan confronted David.
David confessed, "I have sinned against the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:13).
Psalm 51 gives voice to the deep repentance associated with David's sin.
And still, the consequences of his actions were devastating.
Forgiveness did not mean the damage was imaginary.
Grace did not mean accountability disappeared.
This is a truth the Church must never forget.
No spiritual title, ministry position, family reputation, or public success places anyone above God's moral law.
And those harmed by another person's sin must never be pressured to minimize injustice in the name of grace.
God's mercy is not an excuse for the powerful to escape responsibility.
It is the hope of sinners who genuinely repent and turn to Him.
Yet Matthew includes David.
He includes Solomon.
And he reminds us of Uriah.
Because the coming of Jesus was not dependent on the moral perfection of Israel's greatest king.
It depended on the faithfulness of the God who made the promise.
There is something breathtaking about that.
David's sin was real.
God's judgment was real.
God's mercy was real.
And God's covenant purpose continued.
Not because David deserved it.
But because God remained faithful.
Now imagine reading Matthew's genealogy as someone whose own family history is filled with broken promises.
You know what betrayal looks like.
You know how one person's selfish decision can affect an entire household.
You know that a single generation can leave wounds the next generation spends years trying to understand.
And you wonder whether the damage is too deep.
Whether your children will inherit nothing but your failures.
Whether the mistakes of the past have already decided the future.
Matthew does not promise that every earthly consequence will disappear.
But he points us to a Savior whose coming demonstrates that God's redemptive purpose is greater than the sinfulness of the people through whom history unfolded.
Then the genealogy moves through the kings of Judah.
Some pursued the Lord.
Others led the nation into idolatry and injustice.
There were moments of reform.
There were seasons of rebellion.
There were warnings from prophets.
There were judgments that could no longer be postponed.
And then came Babylon.
"And Josias begat Jechonias and his brethren, about the time they were carried away to Babylon." — Matthew 1:11 (KJV)
The exile was not a minor historical inconvenience.
It represented the collapse of Judah's kingdom, the loss of Jerusalem, the destruction of the temple, and the painful consequences of prolonged covenant unfaithfulness.
For the people of Judah, exile raised agonizing questions.
Had God abandoned them?
Had the promises failed?
Would David's royal line ever matter again?
Had the story reached its end?
But Matthew continues.
"And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel." — Matthew 1:12 (KJV)
The names keep coming.
Even after exile.
Even after judgment.
Even after everything seemed lost.
The genealogy continues toward Christ.
That does not mean exile was painless.
It means exile was not the final chapter of God's covenant story.
And perhaps that is the word someone needs today.
You have experienced a season that felt like exile.
Not necessarily because you committed some terrible sin, but because life became unfamiliar and painful.
You lost a relationship.
You buried someone you loved.
You watched a dream collapse.
You found yourself living in circumstances you never imagined.
And somewhere in the darkness, you began to wonder whether God was still at work.
Matthew's genealogy reminds us that long periods of silence are not proof that God has forgotten His promises.
Between the great events of biblical history, ordinary generations lived and died.
Many names are barely known to us beyond their appearance in the genealogy.
But they were not absent from God's knowledge.
And the promised Messiah came at the appointed time.
There is another detail that deserves careful attention.
Matthew arranges the genealogy around three groups of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile, and from the exile to Christ (Matthew 1:17).
This is a deliberate literary and theological structure.
The Hebrew name David is written דָּוִד — David (often represented by the consonants D-W-D).
In traditional Hebrew letter-number values, those consonants add up to fourteen: dalet is four, vav is six, and dalet is four.
Many biblical scholars therefore see Matthew's repeated emphasis on fourteen as a possible way of highlighting David and Jesus' royal identity.
That explanation is plausible, though Matthew does not explicitly state it.
It is also important to understand that ancient genealogies could be selective.
Matthew's genealogy does not list every generation found in the Old Testament royal records. For example, several kings known from Chronicles are omitted between Joram and Uzziah.
This does not mean Matthew accidentally forgot them.
His genealogy is a carefully arranged presentation of Jesus' ancestry and messianic credentials, not a modern exhaustive family register.
And Matthew's account differs in significant ways from the genealogy in Luke 3:23–38.
Christians have proposed different explanations for those differences, including legal and biological lines of descent, but the text does not settle every historical question.
We should not pretend certainty where Scripture has not supplied it.
What Matthew unmistakably emphasizes is this:
Jesus is the promised Messiah.
The Son of Abraham.
The Son of David.
The fulfillment of God's redemptive promises.
And now comes perhaps the most extraordinary turn in the entire passage.
For generation after generation, Matthew repeats a familiar pattern.
Abraham begat Isaac.
Isaac begat Jacob.
Jacob begat Judah.
The fathers are named.
The sons follow.
The genealogy moves forward.
Then Matthew reaches Joseph.
And suddenly, the wording changes.
"And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." — Matthew 1:16 (KJV)
Read it carefully.
Matthew does not say Joseph begat Jesus.
He calls Joseph the husband of Mary.
And then says Jesus was born of Mary.
In the Greek text, the relative pronoun ἧς (hēs), translated "of whom," is feminine singular.
Grammatically, it refers to Mary.
Not Joseph.
Not Joseph and Mary together.
Mary.
This is no insignificant detail.
Matthew's wording prepares the reader for the explanation that follows in Matthew 1:18–25: Jesus was conceived through the work of the Holy Spirit.
Joseph was Jesus' legal father within the household, but Matthew does not present him as Jesus' biological father.
Jesus entered a real human family.
He was born of Mary.
He was publicly connected to the Davidic line through Joseph.
And His conception was miraculous.
The genealogy leads to a birth unlike every birth it has previously recorded.
Here is the wonder of the incarnation.
The eternal Son of God did not remain distant from human history.
He entered it.
He did not come as a sinner.
He came as the sinless Savior.
He was not morally contaminated by the sins of His ancestors.
He came to redeem sinners.
Hebrews 4:15 declares that He was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
Second Corinthians 5:21 teaches that He knew no sin.
First Peter 2:22 says He committed no sin.
This distinction matters.
The message is not that Jesus was just another flawed member of a dysfunctional family.
The message is that the holy Son of God entered a fallen world to accomplish what fallen humanity could never accomplish for itself.
And that brings us to the question beneath every name in Matthew's genealogy.
Why did Jesus come through a family line that included kings, outsiders, and complicated stories?
Because the Messiah came in fulfillment of God's promises within real human history.
Because God's covenant faithfulness endured through generations of human weakness and rebellion.
Because His saving purpose was never limited to people who looked impressive, respectable, or socially acceptable.
Because the Gospel would ultimately bring together Jews and Gentiles through faith in Christ.
And because the One at the center of the genealogy did not come merely to inherit a throne.
He came to save His people from their sins.
Matthew tells us that explicitly only a few verses later.
"And thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins." — Matthew 1:21 (KJV)
There it is.
The heart of the story.
Not merely ancestry.
Not merely history.
Not merely the survival of a royal family line.
Salvation.
The name Jesus comes from the Hebrew name יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua), associated with the meaning "The LORD saves."
And Matthew immediately explains His mission.
He will save His people from their sins.
Not simply from embarrassment.
Not merely from painful memories.
Not just from the consequences of bad decisions.
From sin itself.
From guilt before a holy God.
From the judgment we deserve.
And through His death and resurrection, He opens the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
This is why we must never reduce the genealogy to a comforting slogan that says, "Your past doesn't matter."
Your past may matter deeply.
The people you hurt matter.
The harm done to you matters.
The truth matters.
Justice matters.
Repentance matters.
But your past is not more powerful than the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And that is where the story moves from scandal to grace.
Not cheap grace that excuses evil.
Not sentimental grace that avoids uncomfortable truth.
But the costly grace of the Gospel.
The grace that required the cross.
The grace that confronts our sin and offers forgiveness through the crucified and risen Savior.
The grace that does not leave us where it finds us.
Some of us want God to remove the consequences of sin without changing our hearts.
We want relief without repentance.
Comfort without surrender.
Forgiveness without confession.
A Savior who rescues us from pain but never challenges our pride.
Yet Jesus came to save us from our sins, not to make peace with them.
And the same Gospel that welcomes the repentant sinner also calls that sinner into a transformed life.
That is why the genealogy is so powerful.
It is not a celebration of human brokenness.
It is a testimony to divine faithfulness.
It shows us that God can accomplish His holy purposes in a world filled with unholy people.
But the decisive answer to sin is not found in the genealogy itself.
It is found in the Jesus to whom the genealogy leads.
The baby born in Bethlehem would grow up.
He would proclaim the kingdom of God.
He would welcome repentant sinners.
He would confront religious hypocrisy.
He would heal the sick.
He would show compassion to the overlooked.
He would call people to turn from sin and follow Him.
And He would go to the cross.
There, the true King would wear a crown of thorns.
The sinless Son would suffer for sinners.
The One who fulfilled the promises to Abraham and David would give His life as a ransom for many.
And on the third day, He would rise again.
The genealogy begins with names from the past.
But the Gospel moves toward a living Savior.
And now the question becomes personal.
Not whether your family tree is impressive.
Not whether people approve of your background.
Not whether your reputation is spotless.
But whether you have turned to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
Because being related to religious people does not save you.
Growing up in a Christian household does not save you.
Knowing biblical history does not save you.
Having a respectable family name does not save you.
Jesus saves.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not reserved for people who have managed to keep their lives looking perfect.
It is for sinners who recognize their need for mercy.
For the proud who are willing to humble themselves.
For the ashamed who are ready to come into the light.
For the wounded who need the comfort of Christ.
For the spiritually exhausted who have been trying to carry burdens they were never meant to carry alone.
For the person who has spent years hiding behind a carefully maintained image.
For the one who thinks, "If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again."
Jesus already knows the truth.
And His call is still to repent, believe, and follow Him.
You do not have to manufacture a respectable past before coming to Christ.
You come to Him truthfully.
You confess what needs to be confessed.
You turn from what needs to be abandoned.
You seek to make right what can be made right.
And you trust the mercy of the Savior who died and rose again.
Perhaps you have been carrying shame that Christ is calling you to surrender.
Perhaps you have been excusing a sin that He is calling you to repent of.
Perhaps you have been treating someone else's past as though it permanently disqualifies them from receiving God's mercy.
Or perhaps you have spent so long trying to hide your own story that you have forgotten how to be honest before God.
Do not let this become another article you read, admire, and forget.
Open Matthew 1 again.
Read the names slowly.
Remember the stories.
Remember the warnings.
Remember the promises.
And then look at Jesus.
Because every name ultimately points beyond itself to Him.
You do not need to reveal private wounds or confess personal details publicly. God hears the prayers that never appear in a comment section.
But your words may encourage someone else who has been afraid to seek His mercy.
And perhaps there is someone you know who needs to read this.
A brother who believes his past has disqualified him.
A sister who has been crushed by shame.
A parent who worries that family mistakes have destroyed the future.
A friend who has walked away from church because they encountered judgment without compassion.
A believer who has forgotten the difference between grace and permission to continue in sin.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to join us in opening the Scriptures and considering the claims of Jesus Christ.
Because this is more than a collection of inspirational words.
Our desire is to help people know the Savior revealed in God's Word.
And that mission needs more than an audience.
It needs people willing to help sustain it.
Not out of guilt.
Not because giving money makes someone more faithful than a believer who cannot afford to give.
But because sharing in the work of spreading biblical truth is one meaningful way Christians can express generosity and love.
Paul wrote:
"For we are labourers together with God." — 1 Corinthians 3:9 (KJV)
In its context, Paul was speaking of God's servants working together under Him in the ministry of the Gospel.
And Scripture also teaches that believers may voluntarily support those who faithfully labor in teaching and ministry (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving must be willing, not compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It is not a required biblical tithe, and it should never replace your responsibilities to your family, your local church, or those in genuine need.
It can help us keep making resources available to those who may not have the means to purchase them.
That library is part of the mission.
To make biblical nourishment more accessible.
To encourage spiritual growth.
To point people beyond temporary inspiration toward lasting discipleship.
Jesus Christ is.
You are not less valuable because you cannot give financially.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And God's grace cannot be purchased.
But before you leave, I want to bring you back to the very first page of Matthew.
To the names.
To the generations.
To the kings who failed.
To the outsiders who believed.
To the families who suffered.
To the exile that seemed like the end.
To the promises that endured.
And finally, to Jesus.
Imagine if Matthew had hidden every uncomfortable detail.
Imagine if the record had been edited to make every ancestor appear honorable.
Imagine if every difficult name had disappeared.
We might have received a more flattering family history.
But we would have missed something important about the faithfulness of God.
He did not need a flawless collection of human ancestors to bring the sinless Savior into the world.
He kept His promises in the middle of real history.
And the Savior who came is able to redeem real sinners.
Not imaginary people with imaginary problems.
Real people.
People with grief.
People with regrets.
People who have sinned.
People who have been sinned against.
People whose stories include chapters they never wanted.
People who desperately need mercy.
People like us.
That is why the genealogy matters.
It reminds us that the Christian faith is not built on the illusion that human beings are naturally good enough to save themselves.
It is built on the astonishing truth that God sent His Son to save those who could not save themselves.
So when you read Matthew 1 again, do not stop at the scandal.
Do not stop at the failure.
Do not stop at the brokenness.
Follow the names all the way to Jesus.
Because the center of the Christian story is not the shame of the people who came before Him.
It is the glory of the Savior who came for us.
And if you have never truly surrendered your life to Christ, you can begin by turning to Him now.
You can pray in your own words, acknowledging your sin, asking for His mercy, confessing your faith in His death and resurrection, and committing yourself to follow Him.
A prayer is not a magical formula.
Salvation rests in Jesus Christ, not in the perfection of our words.
But the Lord calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
And if you already belong to Christ, let this genealogy deepen your gratitude.
You were not saved because your history was spotless.
You were saved because your Savior is holy, merciful, and faithful.
His grace is not a reason to remain unchanged.
It is the reason you can begin to walk in newness of life.
One day, people may forget the labels they placed on you.
They may forget your achievements.
They may forget your failures.
They may even forget your name.
But what matters eternally is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
And that is the final invitation of Matthew's genealogy.
Do not merely admire the family tree.
Come to the Savior.

Because the greatest miracle in this family tree is not that God preserved a line of imperfect people — it is that the sinless Jesus entered their history to offer sinners a future they could never earn.
